**Cancer Immunotherapy: Definition and State of the Art**

**1. Defining Cancer Immunotherapy**
Cancer immunotherapy is a therapeutic paradigm that harnesses, enhances, or modifies a patient's own immune system to recognize and eliminate malignant cells, rather than directly targeting the tumor with cytotoxic agents. This approach is fundamentally distinct from traditional chemotherapy and radiotherapy because it modulates the immune microenvironment and can produce durable, "living-drug" responses. The principal classifications of immunotherapy include **immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs)**, **adoptive cell transfer** (e.g., CAR-T cells, TCR-T cells, TILs), **cancer vaccines**, **oncolytic viruses**, **cytokines**, and **bispecific T-cell engagers (BiTEs)**. Mechanistically, ICIs release the "brakes" on exhausted T cells, adoptive transfer engineers and expands tumor-reactive lymphocytes ex vivo, vaccines stimulate antigen-specific immunity, and oncolytic viruses mediate direct tumor destruction while eliciting systemic antitumor immune responses.

**2. State of the Art in Checkpoint Blockade, Vaccines, and AI-Driven Personalization**
First-generation ICIs targeting CTLA-4, PD-1, and PD-L1 remain the backbone of standard care, but the frontier has shifted toward **next-generation checkpoints** (LAG-3, TIGIT, TIM-3) and **bispecific antibodies** designed to block two pathways simultaneously. While monotherapy against LAG-3, TIGIT, and TIM-3 has suffered high-profile Phase III setbacks (e.g., RELATIVITY-098, SKYSCRAPER-02, COSTAR Lung), bispecific constructs such as rilvegostomig (PD-1 × TIGIT) are showing encouraging early efficacy in metastatic NSCLC. A parallel SOTA breakthrough is the integration of ICIs with **personalized mRNA neoantigen vaccines**. In the Phase 3 INTerpath-001 trial, adding intismeran autogene to adjuvant pembrolizumab in resected stage IIB–IV melanoma reduced the risk of recurrence or death by **42%** (HR 0.58) versus pembrolizumab alone, with a 24-month recurrence-free survival rate of 82.2% versus 70%. Complementing these clinical advances, **AI-driven multi-omics** platforms are now being used to predict optimal chemo-immunotherapy combinations, classify tumors into immunotherapy-sensitive subtypes, and guide real-time treatment adaptation by integrating genomic, transcriptomic, and tumor-microenvironment features.

**3. State of the Art in Engineered Cell Therapies and Solid-Tumor Breakthroughs**
CAR-T therapy has transformed hematologic malignancies, but solid tumors remain the field's defining challenge due to **antigen heterogeneity**, an **immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME)**, poor T-cell infiltration, and on-target/off-tumor toxicity. The SOTA response is **"armored" CAR-T cells** engineered to secrete immune-stimulating cytokines—such as IL-12 or IL-18—locally upon tumor engagement, thereby reprogramming the TME and restoring antitumor immunity. Clinical proof-of-concept has been achieved with **IL-15-armored GPC3 CAR-T cells**: in a first-in-human study, IL-15 co-expression significantly increased CAR-T expansion and produced a **33% antitumor response rate** and **66% disease control rate** in solid cancers, with cytokine release syndrome rapidly controlled by an **inducible caspase-9 safety switch**. Beyond CAR-T, **bispecific T-cell engagers (BiTEs)** have crossed the hematology–solid-tumor divide, with FDA approvals of tebentafusp (uveal melanoma) and tarlatamab (small cell lung cancer) establishing proof of concept in solid malignancies. The next frontier is **logic-gated CAR designs** such as the **Tmod™ system**, which combines an activating CAR against a tumor antigen (e.g., mesothelin) with an inhibitory receptor recognizing HLA-A*02 on normal cells; this AND-NOT logic enables selective tumor killing while sparing healthy tissue, and is now entering Phase 1/2 trials (EVEREST-2) with an inducible membrane-tethered IL-12 booster to enhance potency without systemic toxicity.

When ordinary Markdown is enough, when a Quarto source earns its place, and how both end up as the same kind of page at the same kind of address. A synthetic demonstration.
Having read the two other demonstrations, or having written a Markdown article

A reader of The Greenhouse cannot tell how an article was written, and should not need to. Behind a page there may be a Markdown file or a Quarto document. This article is about that difference: why there are two formats, what each is good for, and what keeps them from becoming two websites.

## Two sources, one kind of page

Both formats become the same thing: one entry in the collection, with one address, one set of metadata and one layout. The reader sees the same header, the same type, the same contents list beside the text and the same way on to the next article. You can check this yourself by opening [A Small Guide to Scientific Markdown](/lecture-notes/greenhouse/demo-scientific-markdown/), which is a Markdown file, and [From Synthetic Signals to Reproducible Results](/lecture-notes/greenhouse/demo-synthetic-signals/), which is a Quarto document, one after the other.

| | Markdown | Quarto |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Source file | `name.md` in the collection | `name.qmd` in `science/` |
| Where the metadata is written | Its own front matter | Its own front matter |
| Who builds the body | Astro | Quarto, then a strict check |
| Code | Shown, never run | Shown, and run when you ask |
| Equations, figures, citations | Written by hand | Numbered and cross-referenced |
| Needs extra tools to build the site | No | No: the result is committed |
| Needs extra tools to write | No | Quarto, and Python for computed cells |

## When Markdown is enough

Most articles are made of explanation. A tutorial about a command, a note on a design decision, a worked example with a short snippet: these need headings, lists, code and perhaps a table, and Markdown does all of it with a file you can read in any editor. It builds in seconds and asks nothing of the machine that builds the site. If an article would be fine as plain text with headings, write it as Markdown.

## When Quarto earns its place

A scientific article makes promises that prose alone cannot keep. Figure 3 must still be Figure 3 after a section is added before it. An equation referred to as the model must be the equation that is printed. A citation must appear in the bibliography, and a number in the text must be the number the code produced. Quarto keeps these promises mechanically:

1. Numbered figures, tables and equations are labelled, and every reference to them is a link that cannot go stale.
2. Citations are written as keys and checked against a bibliography file, which prints the reference list.
3. Code cells run in a recorded environment, and the figure or table is made *from* the code rather than pasted beside it.

## How both reach the same site

The site, its folders, its addresses and its layouts belong to Astro. Quarto never builds the site. It prepares one article at a time, and a script then checks what Quarto produced against a short list of what an article may contain: no scripts, no page chrome, no images from elsewhere, no unresolved reference. What survives is stored beside the entry as a plain fragment of HTML. From there it is the same path as a Markdown article: the entry's metadata decides whether it is published, its slug decides its address, and its collection decides its layout.

## Computation is not part of building

The most important separation is the least visible. Building the site never runs a computation. A Quarto document with code is executed only when its author asks, in a prepared environment, with a fixed random seed, and the results are stored with the article. The site build only checks that the stored results are still the ones the current code would produce, by comparing fingerprints. If the code or the data changed and the results did not, the build stops and says which document is stale. A figure on the page is therefore never newer or older than the code beside it without anybody noticing.

## A short rule of thumb

- Writing about something: Markdown.
- Showing a result that code produced, or that readers should be able to reproduce: Quarto.
- Unsure: start in Markdown. A Markdown article can be moved to Quarto when it earns it; nothing is lost.

How an ordinary Markdown file becomes a Greenhouse article: the structure to write, what the page builds from it, and where Markdown stops being enough. A synthetic demonstration.
Having written a plain text file

A Markdown article is a text file that says what its parts are and leaves the look to the site. This guide is itself one: the file you are reading is a few hundred lines of plain text, and everything on the page, the contents list beside it, the header, the dates and the way on to the next article, was built from it by the same code that will build every real article of The Greenhouse.

## The idea in one paragraph

You write headings, paragraphs, lists, code and tables. You describe the article once, at the top of the file, in a few lines of metadata. The site decides the typography, the width of the text and where the contents list goes. A good Markdown article therefore has very little to say about appearance and a lot to say about *structure*.

> The best formatting is the one a reader never notices.
> Structure first; the page does the rest.

## The parts of an article

### The metadata block

The block at the top of the file, between the two lines of dashes, is the article's passport. It gives the title, a one-line description, a publication state, a slug that becomes the last part of the address, and optional fields such as tags and a level.

| Field | Required | What it is for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `title` | yes | The one `<h1>` of the page |
| `description` | when published | The summary under the title and in lists |
| `status` | yes | `draft`, `published` or `archived` |
| `slug` | yes | The address: it never comes from the title |
| `publishedAt` | when published | The date shown with the article |
| `difficulty` | no | `introductory`, `intermediate` or `advanced` |
| `prerequisites` | no | What a reader should know first |

A draft has no page in a production build. It is routed only on a developer's own computer, so an unfinished article is never published by accident.

### Headings

The title is the page's one top-level heading, so the body starts at `##`. Sections use `##`, their parts use `###`. The site reads these headings to build the contents list; an article with fewer than three of them has no list, because a short text does not need one.

### Lists, emphasis and code

Prefer lists when the items are parallel:

1. State the question.
2. Show the smallest example that works.
3. Say where it stops working.

Use *emphasis* for a word that carries stress, **strong** text rarely, and `inline code` for anything a reader might type. For several lines, use a fenced block and name its language:

```python
# A minimal example: the mean of a list, with the standard library only.
from statistics import fmean

readings = [4.2, 3.9, 4.4, 4.1]
print(f"mean of {len(readings)} readings: {fmean(readings):.2f}")  # a deliberately long line, to show that code scrolls inside its box instead of widening the page
```

A long line stays on one line and scrolls inside its box, so the page itself never moves sideways.

## Links

An internal link names a page of this site: [the Greenhouse](/lecture-notes/greenhouse/) is the folder that holds long technical articles, and [the next demonstration](/lecture-notes/greenhouse/demo-synthetic-signals/) shows what the same article looks like when it also has equations, a computed figure and a bibliography. An external link, such as [the CommonMark specification](https://spec.commonmark.org/), leaves the site.

## Where Markdown is enough, and where it is not

Markdown is enough when the article is made of words, lists, short code and tables. It stops being enough when the article needs numbered equations, figures produced by code, cross-references that must not break, or citations that build their own bibliography. For those, GusmaoLab accepts an optional Quarto source for the same collection; the comparison is the subject of [One Archive, Two Authoring Formats](/lecture-notes/greenhouse/demo-markdown-and-quarto/).

## A checklist before publishing

- The title says what the article is about, not that it is an article.
- The description is one sentence a stranger could read in a list.
- Every heading is a heading, and every heading level is used in order.
- Every link goes where it says.
- The slug is final, because it is the address.
